extracted.intended_audience: writers of humour, satirists, and conversationalists (general literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing humorous essays, satirical pieces, and witty conversation — including how to handle self-reference, characterisation, innuendo, and reader-engagement techniques common to early-18th-century periodical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reference in humour
rubrics_metrics.description: "In Works of Humour, especially when a Man writes under a fictitious Personage, the talking of one's self may give some Diversion to the Publick; but I would advise every other Writer never to speak of himself, unless there be something very considerable in his Character."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit personal talk chiefly when writing under a fictitious persona or when the writer's own character is genuinely interesting; otherwise avoid speaking of oneself as it distracts from the humour and appears vain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming old jests as your own
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticises "those empty conceited Fellows, who repeat as Sayings of their own ... several Jests which were made before they were born," calling this an absurdity of egotists in conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not appropriate well-known or previously printed jokes as original material — it marks shallowness. Remedy: read widely (e.g., joke collections like the 'Oxford and Cambridge Jests') so you recognise old conceits and avoid repeating them as new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray characters with mixed virtues and vices
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is indeed no such thing as a Person entirely good or bad; Virtue and Vice are blended and mixed together..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing people to simple extremes in depiction. For more truthful, interesting humour and moral point, present characters as mixtures of qualities; this yields subtler comic or satirical results and avoids caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh circumstances before moral judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Argues that actions often require careful weighing: the same action may be difficult to determine 'whether it ought to be rewarded or punish'd' and cites legal maxims and the Spartan anecdote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using moral judgement for satire or comedic critique, consider surrounding context and unintended consequences; nuanced treatment is often more just and more interesting than blunt condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scandalous or provocative keywords to attract readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation: 'few Writings sell which are not filled with great Names and illustrious Titles' and that 'A sprinkling of the Words Faction, Frenchman, Papist, Plunderer,... have also a very good Effect upon the Eye of the Purchaser.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategically include striking, controversial, or charged terms to draw reader attention and sales. This is a pragmatic tactic for periodical writing — effective but ethically debatable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ redaction/obscuration (dashes, asterisks, blanks) for innuendo
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes the practice of putting dashes/asterisks or omitting vowels (e.g., 'M--lborough', omitting vowels to 'gutted a proper Name') to create insinuation and reader engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Masking names or terms with dashes/asterisks/vowel-omission creates a teasing innuendo that invites readers to decode and feel clever; it also provides plausible deniability against libel while heightening interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use puzzles/enigmas and reader participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Says masked names and gaps 'give a secret Satisfaction to a Peruser ... that he is able to decipher them without help' and offers to print explanations of an enigma if a reader solves it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage readers by embedding decodeable puzzles or incomplete references; invite solutions or submissions to increase interaction and loyalty. This technique converts passive readers into active participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate fashionable devices (syncopation of words) to suit audience taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Mocks and records contemporary 'Syncopists' who write with omitted letters and dashes, and suggests matching such devices to 'thoroughly content my English Readers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of prevailing stylistic devices that please your audience (e.g., syncopated or partly-censored political jabs) and adopt them intentionally when appropriate to taste and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small social rituals to open conversation and camaraderie
rubrics_metrics.description: "Lighting a Man's Pipe at the same Candle, is looked upon among Brother-smokers as an Overture to Conversation and Friendship."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In spoken wit and coffee-house humour, use small shared gestures or rituals as conversational openings; such cues create rapport and permit freer humorous exchange.
